scenes.text: What actually stops an elevator from falling? Let's cut the shaft open. The car hangs from at least three steel ropes, and together they're built many times stronger than the load. A heavy counterweight balances the car, so the motor only lifts the difference. Up top, the motor has a brake that works backwards. Springs squeeze it shut all the time, and electricity pulls it open. So if the power goes out, the brake clamps on by itself. But what if every rope snapped? Here's the clever part. A second, thinner rope loops from the car up to a wheel called the governor. Inside that wheel are spinning weights. Spin too fast, and the weights fly outward, catch, and lock the wheel. The thin rope stops, the car keeps dropping, so the rope yanks a lever on the car. That lever jams steel wedges against the guide rails on both sides, and the car's own weight drives them in tighter. The car grinds to a stop on the rails, no rope needed. Still not enough? At the bottom of the shaft sit buffers, big springs or oil pistons that catch the car. This whole idea goes back to 1854. In New York, a mechanic named Elisha Otis rode a platform high above a crowd, and had the rope cut. The platform held. Do you trust the elevator, or do you take the stairs? Tell me in the comments. If you found this useful, don't forget to follow.
